🇲🇽📈 <u>DELOITTE: MEXICO HEADED FOR HISTORIC EXPORT BOOM IN 2026</u>

Even the private sector's cautious voices concede it: Mexico is on track for a historic export boom this year, tariffs and all. Deloitte's Econosignal report shows high-value manufacturing surging — electronic components up 10.6% annually, aerospace up 16.2% — while it forecasts 1.2% GDP growth and notes national content in exports sits at 44%, stuck at 2015 levels. Fair warning, and exactly what Plan México's industrial policy is built to fix. The boom is real; the task now is to make it more Mexican.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>NYT AND US CONGRESS RESEARCH CONFIRM SHEINBAUM ON VISAS</u>

Days after Washington revoked visas from Morena figures — including AMLO's son — the US establishment's own sources say Mexico was right. A New York Times analysis and a Congressional Research Service report confirm the Trump administration has sharply expanded the use of visa cancellations as political pressure across Latin America, tied to Washington's strategic disputes; Le Monde documented the same pattern, down to Brazil's ambassador in Washington losing hers. Sheinbaum called it immediately: the revocations have "an essentially political purpose... a sense of interference in Mexican politics." Now it's in the CRS record.

🇲🇽🗂️ <u>SHEINBAUM: THE DFS DIDN'T JUST SPY — IT TORTURED AND DISAPPEARED</u>

Asked by Contralínea about Mexico's real authoritarian past, President Sheinbaum was blunt: the DFS "didn't just investigate politicians and social leaders — it detained them, tortured them and disappeared them." She speaks from experience: the political police opened a file on her as a child. Today the right cries "authoritarianism" over audience-rights rules and an elected judiciary. "They criticize us as authoritarians," she said, "but they've forgotten all that."

🔥🇲🇽 <u>PRI'S POLITICAL POLICE TRACKED SALINAS' RISE, ARCHIVES SHOW</u>

The National Archive keeps delivering. Master copies from the DFS and the DGIPS — the PRI regime's political police — show Carlos Salinas de Gortari was spied on for years as he climbed from the Budget Ministry to the 1988 succession: hundreds of index cards, memos and reports logging his meetings, tours and decisions while Mexico was shoved from the welfare state into neoliberalism. The same apparatus that tortured dissidents was taking notes on the man who would later sign NAFTA. The archives don't forget.

🇲🇽📊 <u>INEGI: 85% OF MEXICAN KIDS AGED 6-14 ARE NOW ONLINE</u>

Mexico's digital inclusion keeps closing gaps: INEGI's 2025 Endutih survey puts internet use at 85.4% among children aged 6 to 14 — up from 63.3% in 2015 — and at 97.6% among those aged 15 to 24. Access is nearly universal; the battle now is over what happens on the screen. Kids aged 12-17 average 4.5 hours a day connected, and researchers warn childhoods are being turned "into algorithms for the big tech companies, which see them not as rights-holders but as merchandise." That is the logic behind Mexico's push: reading programs in schools and rules on screens.

🇲🇽🇨🇳 <u>SINALOA SELLS CHINA UP TO 1.2 MILLION TONS OF SORGHUM</u>

While Washington threatens tariffs, Mexico keeps opening markets. Sinaloa just signed a letter of intent with China's Sichuan Yourong Group for up to 1.2 million tons of red sorghum, with the first five containers leaving the port of Topolobampo for quality tests — the grain is headed for baijiu, China's national liquor. The buyers tested it against Australian sorghum and came back sold: "Today we can say we believe we have found the best sorghum in the world." Diversification is not a speech. It is cargo leaving Topolobampo.

🇲🇽📊 <u>MEXICO'S POVERTY LINE HITS 4,884 PESOS AS FOOD COSTS OUTRUN INFLATION</u>

Per El Economista's weekly data wrap: INEGI's July poverty lines put the basic basket of food and services at 4,884.09 pesos per person in urban Mexico, up 3.5% annually — running above the 3.1% headline inflation. The food-only threshold rose 3.8% in the cities to 2,545.72 pesos, driven by meals away from home (+6.0%) and potatoes, up 62.3% in a year.

The official yardstick for what it costs not to be poor keeps rising faster than the CPI.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>MEXICO'S PHONE REGISTRY TOPS 71 MILLION LINES AS FIRST CUTOFF TAKES EFFECT</u>

Mexico's CRT confirmed there would be no extension: unregistered mobile lines ending in 0 began losing service this weekend, with the shutdown rolling out gradually over 72 hours. Suspended numbers are not lost — service restores automatically once the owner completes registration, at no cost and with no balance required.

71 million lines are already verified in the national registry, built to choke off extortion calls.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>79% OF MEXICANS BACK SANCTIONS ON MEDIA THAT DECEIVE AUDIENCES</u>

Mexico's corporate media spent two weeks crying censorship over the audience-rights guidelines. A new De Las Heras poll: 79% of Mexicans believe the government should sanction outlets that deceive audiences with false information, and 78% want a clear line between news and paid content. Only 28% buy the censorship narrative.

Sheinbaum stressed her guidelines propose neither sanctions nor content control — just ethics codes and ombudsmen to handle audience complaints: "Como decía el presidente López Obrador: tonto es el que cree que el pueblo es tonto."
